subject: maths
title: Interpreting Data: Comparing Data Sets, Mode, Range and Misleading Graphs
seo_title: Year 6 Interpreting Data Worksheets: Mode, Range, Dot Plots and Misleading Graphs (Free, Answer Key)
standard_text: Interpret and compare data sets for ordinal and nominal categorical, discrete and continuous numerical variables using comparative displays or visualisations and digital tools; compare distributions in terms of mode, range and shape
meta_desc: Free Year 6 maths worksheets on interpreting data for the Australian Curriculum (AC9M6ST01, AC9M6ST02): kinds of data, side-by-side column graphs and dot plots, mode and range, comparing two data sets, and spotting misleading graphs and claims in the media. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Compare data sets using the mode, the range and the shape.
key_sub: The mode is the value that appears most often. Range = highest − lowest. Before you trust a graph or a claim, check that the scale starts at 0 and ask how many people were asked, and who.
body_html:
Kinds of data

First decide what kind of data you have. Categorical data is words or labels. Numerical data is numbers you count or measure.

Kind of dataWhat the answers areExample
Nominal categoricalCategories with no orderFavourite sport, numbers on footy jumpers
Ordinal categoricalCategories with an orderShirt size S, M, L; gold, silver, bronze
Discrete numericalNumbers you count (whole numbers)Number of pets, goals in a game
Continuous numericalNumbers you measure (any value)Height in cm, time for 100 m

Mode and range

The mode is the value that appears most often. The range is highest value − lowest value. A small range means the data is close together. A large range means it is spread out.

Example 1

Find the mode and the range for 6D.

The tallest stack is above 5, so the mode is 5 laps. Highest 7, lowest 3, so the range is 7 − 3 = 4 laps.

Answer: mode 5 laps, range 4 laps

Example 2

Compare the shapes of the two classes.

6D is bunched in the middle (3 to 7, range 4). 6E is spread out from 1 to 8 (range 7), with the most dots at 7 and 8.

Answer: 6D is more consistent; 6E is more spread out

To compare two sets of data, use the mode, the range and the shape: where most of the data is, any gaps, and any values far from the rest. A side-by-side column graph does the same job for categories: use the key to see which column belongs to which group.

Is the claim supported?

Before you believe a graph in an ad or the news, check three things. Does the scale start at 0? How many people were asked? Who was asked?

Example 3

A sign says, “Everyone loves the new playground: 100% of the kids we asked said yes!” They asked 3 kids. Is the claim supported?

3 kids is far too small a sample to speak for everyone.

Answer: No

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Giving the highest value as the modeThe mode is the value that appears most often
Giving the number of dots as the modeGive the value under the tallest stack, not the stack’s height
Giving the biggest number as the rangeRange = highest − lowest
Using the first and last numbers in a listFind the highest and lowest values first
Judging by column heights when the scale does not start at 0Read the real values and subtract
Trusting a survey of a few people, or of people chosen in one placeAsk how many and who was asked

faq.q: What do Year 6 students learn about data in the Australian Curriculum?
faq.a: In Year 6 students interpret and compare data sets using side-by-side column graphs and dot plots, describe them using the mode, range and shape, and decide whether statistical claims in the media are supported.

faq.q: What is the difference between discrete and continuous data?
faq.a: Discrete data is counted and has whole-number values, such as the number of pets. Continuous data is measured and can be any value in a range, such as height or time.

faq.q: How do you find the range of a set of data?
faq.a: Find the highest value and the lowest value, then subtract: range = highest − lowest. Do not just use the biggest number or the first and last numbers in the list.

faq.q: How can a graph be misleading?
faq.a: A column graph whose scale does not start at 0 makes small differences look big. Claims can also mislead when the sample is very small or the people asked were not chosen fairly.

sets.title: Kinds of data: nominal, ordinal, discrete and continuous

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
Each student’s favourite ice-cream flavour
items.e: The answers are names of flavours, so the data is categorical. Flavours have no natural order, so it is nominal.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The number of brothers and sisters each student has
items.e: The answers are counted: 0, 1, 2, 3 … Counted data with only whole-number values is discrete. (Nobody has 2.5 brothers.)

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
Each student’s height in centimetres
items.e: Height is measured, so it can be any value in a range, such as 148.6 cm. Measured data is continuous.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
Shirt size: S, M, L or XL
items.e: The answers are categories that have a natural order: S is smaller than M, M is smaller than L. They are letters, not counts, so the data is not numerical.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The time each runner takes to run 100 m at the athletics carnival
items.e: Time is measured, and it can be any value, such as 15.37 seconds. So it is continuous numerical data.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The number of goals scored in each netball game
items.e: Goals are counted. You can score 12 or 13 goals but not 12.5, so the data is discrete numerical.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
How students rate the canteen’s new wrap: poor, OK, good or excellent
items.e: The answers are words, so the data is categorical. Poor, OK, good, excellent have an order, so it is ordinal.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The way each student gets to school: walk, bike, car or bus
items.e: The answers are categories with no natural order, so the data is nominal categorical.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The number on each player’s footy jumper
items.e: The numbers are only names for the players. Adding them or putting them in order means nothing, so the data is nominal categorical, even though it looks like numbers.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The mass of each student’s school bag in kilograms
items.e: Mass is measured, so it can be any value, such as 4.35 kg. Measured data is continuous numerical.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The place each swimmer finishes in a race: 1st, 2nd, 3rd …
items.e: The places are categories that tell the order the swimmers finished. They do not count or measure anything, so the data is ordinal categorical.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The rainfall in Darwin each day, in millimetres
items.e: Rainfall is measured, and it can be any value, such as 12.4 mm. So it is continuous numerical data.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The number of students on each school bus
items.e: Students are counted, so the values are whole numbers only. The data is discrete numerical.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The colour of each car in the school car park
items.e: Colours are categories with no natural order, so the data is nominal categorical.

items.q: Which of these is continuous numerical data?
c: The number of pets at home
The amount of water each student drinks in a day (mL)
items.e: Water is measured, so it can be any value in a range. Pets are counted (discrete), sports are nominal and year levels are ordinal.

items.q: Which of these is discrete numerical data?
c: The temperature at 9 am each day
The length of each student’s hair (cm)
The number of books each student read in Term 2
items.e: Books are counted in whole numbers, so the data is discrete. Temperature and length are measured (continuous), and colour is nominal.

items.q: Which of these is ordinal categorical data?
c: The number of people in each family
The medal each athlete won: gold, silver or bronze
The type of pet each student has
items.e: Gold, silver and bronze are categories with an order. Pets have no order (nominal). People are counted and mass is measured, so those are numerical.

items.q: Which of these is nominal categorical data?
c: The state or territory where each student was born
How much students agree: disagree, unsure, agree
The number of cousins each student has
The time each student spends reading
items.e: States and territories are categories with no natural order, so the data is nominal. Disagree, unsure, agree has an order (ordinal).

items.q: Why is “the time taken to swim 50 m” continuous data?
c: The answers are categories in order
It is measured, so it can be any value in a range
It is counted in whole numbers
items.e: Time is measured, not counted. A swimmer could take 48.2 s or 48.25 s, so any value in a range is possible.

items.q: Ruby counts the people in each car at school drop-off. She also measures how long each car stays. Which is true?
items.e: People are counted in whole numbers (discrete). Time is measured and can be any value (continuous).

sets.title: Side-by-side column graphs and dot plots

items.q: Use the key. How many students in 6B ride a bike?
items.e: 6B is the second (orange) column. The 6B column for Bike ends on the line between 8 and 10, so 9. (5 is 6A.)

items.q: How many students in 6A come by car?
items.e: 6A is the first (green) column. The 6A column for Car reaches 10. (7 is 6B, and 17 is both classes.)

items.q: How many students walk to school altogether, in both classes?
items.e: 6A: 8 walk. 6B: 4 walk. Altogether means add: 8 + 4 = 12. (4 subtracts instead of adds.)

items.q: How many more 6B students than 6A students ride a bike?
items.e: 6B: 9. 6A: 5. How many more means subtract: 9 − 5 = 4.

items.q: For which ways of travel does 6A have more students than 6B?
items.e: Compare the two columns for each way. Walk: 8 and 4. Car: 10 and 7. In both, the green 6A column is taller. For bike and bus the orange 6B column is taller.

items.q: What is the mode for 6B?
items.e: The mode is the category with the tallest column. For 6B (orange) that is Bike, with 9 students. The mode is the category, not the number 9. (Car is the mode for 6A.)

items.q: How many students are in 6A?
items.e: Add all the 6A columns: 8 + 5 + 10 + 3 = 26. (10 is only the tallest column.)

items.q: Using both classes, which way of travel is the most common?
items.e: Add the two classes. Walk 12, bike 14, car 17, bus 9. Car is the most common. (Bike has the tallest single column, but you must add both classes.)

items.q: The scale is labelled in 10s. What is each small square worth?
items.e: There are 5 small squares between 0 and 10. 10 ÷ 5 = 2, so each small square is 2 drinks.

items.q: How many hot chocolates were sold in the week in July?
items.e: July is the orange column. The hot chocolate column reaches the line for 30. (4 is February, and 15 counts each small square as 1.)

items.q: How many bottles of water were sold in the week in February?
items.e: February is the green column. Water ends 2 small squares above 30. Each square is 2, so 30 + 4 = 34. (17 counts each small square as 1, and 16 is July.)

items.q: Which drinks sold more in the July week than in the February week?
items.e: The orange July column is taller for milk (18 and 12) and for hot chocolate (30 and 4). For water and juice, February is taller.

items.q: How many more hot chocolates were sold in the July week than in the February week?
items.e: July: 30. February: 4. 30 − 4 = 26. Hot drinks sell more in winter, which in Australia is June to August.

items.q: What is the mode for the February week?
items.e: The tallest green column is water (34). The mode is the drink, not the number. (Hot chocolate is the mode for July.)

items.q: Each dot is one student. How many students read 4 books?
items.e: Count the dots above 4: there are 5.

items.q: How many students are in 6C?
items.e: Each dot is one student, so count every dot: 2 + 4 + 6 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 23. (84 is the number of books, and 9 is the highest value.)

items.q: How many students read more than 4 books?
items.e: More than 4 means 5, 6 or 9 books: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Students who read exactly 4 do not count.

items.q: One value is far away from the rest. Which value is it?
items.e: The dot at 9 is on its own, with gaps at 7 and 8. All the other dots are from 1 to 6.

items.q: What kind of data is shown in this dot plot?
items.e: The number of books is counted in whole numbers, so it is discrete numerical data.

items.q: Which sentence best describes the shape of the data?
c: The dots are spread out evenly
Every student read at least 2 books
items.e: 4 + 6 + 5 + 3 = 18 of the 23 students read 2, 3, 4 or 5 books. The dots are bunched in the middle, with one far away at 9. (2 students read only 1 book.)

items.q:
Goals scored by the school netball team in 7 games:
12, 18, 9, 12, 11, 12, 10
What is the mode?
items.e: The mode is the value that appears most often. 12 appears 3 times, so the mode is 12 goals. (18 is the highest value, and 3 is how many times 12 appears.)

items.q:
Goals scored by the school netball team in 7 games:
12, 18, 9, 12, 11, 12, 10
What is the range?
items.e: Range = highest − lowest = 18 − 9 = 9 goals. (18 is just the highest value, and 12 − 10 = 2 uses the first and last numbers in the list instead of the highest and lowest. 18 − 12 = 6 uses the mode instead of the lowest value.)

items.q:
Ages of the children at a birthday party:
11, 12, 11, 10, 12, 11, 13
What is the mode?
items.e: 11 appears 3 times, more than any other age, so the mode is 11 years. (13 is the highest age, and 3 is how many times 11 appears.)

items.q:
Masses of 5 dogs at the vet (kg):
31, 25, 40, 28, 36
What is the range?
items.e: Highest 40 kg, lowest 25 kg. Range = 40 − 25 = 15 kg. (36 − 31 = 5 uses the last and first numbers, which are not the highest and lowest. 65 adds instead of subtracts.)

items.q: Each dot is one car. What is the mode?
items.e: The tallest stack is above 2, so the mode is 2 people. (9 is the number of cars, and 5 is the highest value.)

items.q: What is the range of the number of people in each car?
items.e: Range = highest − lowest = 5 − 1 = 4 people. Use the values along the number line, not the heights of the stacks (9 − 1 = 8).

items.q: Each dot is one student. What is the mode?
items.e: The tallest stack (5 dots) is above 16, so the mode is 16. (5 is how many students scored 16.)

items.q: What is the range of the scores?
items.e: Highest score 20, lowest score 12. Range = 20 − 12 = 8. (Nobody scored 13 or 19, but the range only uses the highest and lowest. 5 − 1 = 4 uses the heights of the stacks, and 32 adds.)

items.q:
Shoe sizes of 7 students:
4, 5, 6, 5, 7, 6, 3
What is the mode?
items.e: 5 appears twice and 6 appears twice. Every other size appears once. So there are two modes: 5 and 6.

items.q:
Quiz scores of 5 students:
3, 8, 6, 9, 4
What is the mode?
items.e: Each score appears only once, so no value appears most often. There is no mode. (9 is the highest score, and 5 is how many scores there are.)

items.q:
Long jump distances at the athletics carnival (m):
2.35, 2.8, 3.1, 2.62, 2.9
What is the range?
items.e: Highest 3.1 m, lowest 2.35 m. Line up the decimal points: 3.10 − 2.35 = 0.75 m. (2.9 − 2.35 = 0.55 uses the last value, not the highest.)

items.q:
Temperatures at 6 am in Canberra for one week in July (°C):
−3, 1, −1, 2, −4, 0, 3
What is the range?
items.e: Highest 3 °C, lowest −4 °C. From −4 up to 0 is 4 degrees, and from 0 up to 3 is 3 more: range = 3 − (−4) = 7 °C. (4 − 3 = 1 ignores the minus sign, 3 °C is only the highest value, and 4 °C is only the size of the lowest.)

items.q:
Year 6 voted for the end-of-year excursion.
ExcursionVotes
Zoo8
Beach11
Museum5
Movies10
What is the mode?
items.e: The mode is the category with the most votes. Beach has 11 votes. The mode is Beach, not the number 11.

items.q:
Year 6 voted for the end-of-year excursion.
ExcursionVotes
Zoo8
Beach11
Museum5
Movies10
Isla says, “The range of this data is 11 − 5 = 6.” What is wrong?
c: The places are categorical, so they have no range
items.e: The data is the place each student chose. Places are nominal categories with no order, so there is no highest or lowest place. Range is only for numerical data.

items.q:
This table shows how many brothers and sisters the students in 6D have.
Brothers and sistersStudents
05
111
27
32
51
What is the mode?
items.e: The most students (11) have 1 brother or sister, so the mode is 1. (11 is the number of students, and 5 is the highest value.)

items.q:
This table shows how many brothers and sisters the students in 6D have.
Brothers and sistersStudents
05
111
27
32
51
What is the range of the data?
items.e: Highest value 5, lowest value 0. Range = 5 − 0 = 5. (11 − 1 = 10 uses the student counts, and 5 − 1 = 4 forgets that 0 is a value.)

items.q: The range of 5 test scores is 12. The lowest score is 7. What is the highest score?
items.e: Range = highest − lowest, so highest = lowest + range = 7 + 12 = 19. (12 − 7 = 5 subtracts instead of adds, and 84 multiplies.)

items.q: One more car arrives with 3 people in it. What is the mode now?
items.e: Add one dot above 3: now 6 cars have 3 people. The tallest stack is still above 2 (9 dots), so the mode is still 2 people.

items.q: Which set of data has a range of 10?
items.e: Range = highest − lowest. 4, 14, 9, 7: 14 − 4 = 10. The others: 15 − 10 = 5, 11 − 3 = 8, 11 − 2 = 9. (Having the number 10 in the list does not make the range 10.)

items.q:
Heights of 6 sunflowers (cm):
152, 168, 147, 175, 160, 149
What is the range?
items.e: Highest 175 cm, lowest 147 cm. Range = 175 − 147 = 28 cm. (152 − 149 = 3 uses the first and last values, and 149 is not the lowest.)

sets.title: Compare two sets of data: mode, range and shape

items.e: The tallest stack for 6A is above 8, so the mode is 8. (9 is how many students scored 8, and 10 is the highest score.)
The tallest stack for 6B is above 9 (6 dots), so the mode is 9. (6 is how many students scored 9.)
6A: highest 10, lowest 5. Range = 10 − 5 = 5. (9 − 1 = 8 uses the heights of the stacks.)
6B: highest 10, lowest 2. Range = 10 − 2 = 8. (5 is the range for 6A.)
The range measures how spread out the data is. 6B’s range (8) is bigger than 6A’s (5). The mode does not tell you about the spread.
8 or more means 8, 9 or 10: 3 + 6 + 3 = 12. (9 forgets the students who scored exactly 8, and 16 is 6A.)

c: No: more 6A students scored 8 or more
items.e: One value is not enough. 16 students in 6A scored 8 or more, but only 12 in 6B. Many 6B students scored 6 or less.

c: 6A is spread from 2 to 10; 6B is bunched from 7 to 9
6A is bunched from 7 to 9; 6B is spread from 2 to 10
Both classes are spread out evenly
Both classes are bunched from 7 to 9
items.e: 6A: 6 + 9 + 5 = 20 of 25 dots are at 7, 8 or 9. 6B has dots all the way from 2 to 10, with the most at 9.

items.q: Rainfall is rounded to the nearest 10 mm. Which season is the wettest in Perth?
items.e: Perth is the orange column. The tallest orange column is winter (430 mm). In Australia, winter is June to August.

items.q: What is the average rainfall in Darwin in summer?
items.e: Darwin is the green column. The summer label says 1060 mm. (40 mm is Perth, and 1200 is the top of the scale.)

items.q: What is the range of Darwin’s seasonal rainfall?
items.e: Darwin: highest 1060 mm (summer), lowest 10 mm (winter). Range = 1060 − 10 = 1050 mm. (1060 − 230 = 830 does not use the lowest value, and 1060 − 40 = 1020 uses Perth’s lowest.)

items.q: What is the range of Perth’s seasonal rainfall?
items.e: Perth: highest 430 mm (winter), lowest 40 mm (summer). Range = 430 − 40 = 390 mm. (430 − 140 = 290 does not use the lowest value, and 1050 is Darwin’s range.)

items.q: How much more rain does Perth get than Darwin in winter?
items.e: Winter: Perth 430 mm, Darwin 10 mm. 430 − 10 = 420 mm. (440 adds instead of subtracts.)

items.q: Which sentence correctly compares the two cities?
c: Perth is wetter than Darwin in every season
Both cities get the most rain in winter
Darwin gets about the same rain each season
Darwin’s rain falls mostly in summer; Perth’s mostly in winter
items.e: Darwin’s tallest column is summer (its wet season); its winter is almost dry. Perth’s tallest column is winter. The shapes are opposite.

items.q: About how much more rain does Darwin get in a whole year than Perth?

Points scored by two basketball teams in 6 games:
Kookaburras: 42, 38, 45, 38, 50, 39
Wombats: 30, 55, 41, 55, 36, 47
What is the mode for each team?
items.e: Kookaburras: 38 appears twice. Wombats: 55 appears twice. (50 is the Kookaburras’ highest score, and 2 is how many times each mode appears.)

items.q:
Points scored by two basketball teams in 6 games:
Kookaburras: 42, 38, 45, 38, 50, 39
Wombats: 30, 55, 41, 55, 36, 47
What is the range for each team?
items.e: Kookaburras: 50 − 38 = 12. Wombats: 55 − 30 = 25. (42 − 39 = 3 and 47 − 30 = 17 use the first and last scores, not the highest and lowest.)

items.q:
Points scored by two basketball teams in 6 games:
Kookaburras: 42, 38, 45, 38, 50, 39
Wombats: 30, 55, 41, 55, 36, 47
Which team’s scores are more consistent (closer together)?
items.e: A smaller range means the scores are closer together. The Kookaburras’ range is 12 and the Wombats’ is 25.

items.q:
Points scored by two basketball teams in 6 games:
Kookaburras: 42, 38, 45, 38, 50, 39
Wombats: 30, 55, 41, 55, 36, 47
Which team scored more points altogether in the 6 games?
items.e: Kookaburras: 42 + 38 + 45 + 38 + 50 + 39 = 252. Wombats: 30 + 55 + 41 + 55 + 36 + 47 = 264. 264 − 252 = 12. (55 − 38 = 17 compares the modes, not the totals.)

items.q:
Points scored by two basketball teams in 6 games:
Kookaburras: 42, 38, 45, 38, 50, 39
Wombats: 30, 55, 41, 55, 36, 47
If the Wombats had scored 40 instead of 30 in their first game, what would their range be?
items.e: The scores would be 40, 55, 41, 55, 36, 47. The lowest is now 36, not 40. Range = 55 − 36 = 19. (55 − 40 = 15 forgets the 36, and 10 is only the change in one score.)

sets.title: Is the claim supported? Data in the media

items.q: A juice ad shows this graph. How many kids chose Sunny Squeeze?
items.e: The Sunny Squeeze column reaches the line for 52. (12 is the height above the bottom of the scale, which starts at 40, not 0.)

items.q: How many more kids chose Sunny Squeeze than other brands?
items.e: 52 − 46 = 6 kids. The difference is small, even though one column looks twice as tall.

items.q: The ad says, “Twice as many kids choose Sunny Squeeze!” Is this true?
c: Yes: its column is twice as tall
No: more kids chose other brands
items.e: Twice 46 is 92. Only 52 kids chose Sunny Squeeze. The column only looks twice as tall because the scale starts at 40.

items.q: Why does the graph make the difference look big?
c: The columns are the same colour
items.e: When the scale starts at 40, the bottom part of every column is cut off. The small difference (6 kids) then looks huge.

items.q: To draw a fair column graph of this data, where should the scale start?
items.e: Column heights are only fair to compare when the scale starts at 0. Then the columns would be 52 and 46 high, and look almost the same.

items.q: How many more visitors came to the school fete in 2026 than in 2025?
items.e: 2026: 510. 2025: 480. 510 − 480 = 30 visitors. (60 is the height of the 2026 column above 450, where the scale starts, and 510 is the number of visitors in 2026.)

items.q: The newsletter says, “Our fete crowd doubled in 2026!” Which is true?
items.e: Doubling 480 would give 960 visitors, but only 510 came. The scale starts at 450, which makes the 2026 column look twice as tall.

items.q: A website says, “Kids love broccoli! 3 out of 4 kids we asked said yes.” They asked only 4 kids. Why is this claim weak?
c: The sample is far too small
3 out of 4 is less than half
items.e: 4 kids is a tiny sample. A different 4 kids could give a very different answer. (3 out of 4 is more than half.)

items.q: Which survey gives the best answer to “What is the favourite sport of the Year 6 students at our school?”
items.e: Asking everyone in Year 6 includes all the students. A few friends is too small a sample, and the netball team or footy players will mostly choose their own sport.

items.q: A survey at the beach found that 45 of the 50 people asked love swimming. A headline says, “90% of Australians love swimming!” What is the main problem?
c: People at the beach are likely to like swimming
items.e: The sample is biased: people at the beach were chosen, and they are more likely to enjoy swimming. 45 out of 50 is 90%, but only for those 50 people.

items.q: In the beach survey, 45 of the 50 people asked said they love swimming. What percentage is that?
items.e: 45 out of 50 = 90 out of 100 = 90%. (45% treats 45 out of 50 as if it were out of 100.)

items.q: The principal says, “Most of our Year 6 students come to school by car.” Is this supported by the graph?
c: No: only 17 of the 52 students come by car
Yes: 10 students in 6A come by car
Yes: car has the tallest columns
items.e: Car: 10 + 7 = 17 students. Altogether there are 26 + 26 = 52 students. “Most” means more than half, and 17 is less than 26. Car is the most common way, but it is not most students.

items.q: A travel blog says, “Darwin is always wetter than Perth.” Is this supported?
c: Yes: Darwin’s summer column is the tallest
No: Perth gets more rain in a year
Yes: Darwin gets more rain in a year
No: Perth gets more rain in winter
items.e: In winter Perth averages 430 mm and Darwin only 10 mm. Darwin is wetter over the whole year, but not always.

items.q: A TV ad says, “9 out of 10 dog owners choose Wagz dog food.” Which question best checks this claim?
c: How much does the food cost?
How many dog owners were asked, and how were they chosen?
items.e: A claim like this depends on the sample. If only 10 owners were asked, or they were all at a Wagz shop, the claim is weak.

items.q: The canteen expects to sell the same number of hot chocolates each week as in this July week. How many should it order for 10 winter weeks?
items.e: July week: 30 hot chocolates. 30 × 10 = 300. (40 uses the February week, which is summer, and 260 uses the difference between the weeks.)

items.q: Students who score 9 or more get a merit award. How many awards are given in the two classes altogether?
items.e: 6A: 5 + 2 = 7. 6B: 6 + 3 = 9. Altogether 7 + 9 = 16 awards.

items.q: Kai measured the temperature in Hobart at 3 pm on one day in July. It was 11 °C. He says, “It is always 11 °C in Hobart in July.” Is this supported?
c: No: one reading is not enough data
No: Hobart is warm in July
items.e: One reading on one day cannot tell you about every day. The temperature changes during the day and from day to day.

items.q: A school surveys 200 students and 50 say they walk to school. A poster says, “Half of our students walk to school!” Is this supported?
c: No: 50 out of 200 is a quarter
Yes: 50 is a lot of students
items.e: Half of 200 is 100. 50 out of 200 = 1 out of 4, which is a quarter (25%).

items.q: Charlotte wants to compare the favourite sports of 6A and 6B. Which display is best?
items.e: A side-by-side column graph puts the two classes next to each other for each sport, so they are easy to compare. Sport is categorical, so a dot plot or line graph does not fit.

items.q: The school newsletter says, “6C students read 9 books each in Term 2.” Is this supported?
items.e: Only one dot is above 9. The mode is 3 books, and most students read 2 to 5 books. 84 is the total for the whole class.
